definition: A sudden overwhelming feeling of fear or anxiety that spreads quickly and often leads to wild, unreasoning behavior.
origin: Panic comes from the Greek god Pan, the horned, goat-legged god of shepherds and wild places, whose unexpected shriek from the woods was said to strike travelers and armies with sudden, irrational terror. The Greeks called this sensation panikon (of Pan), and ancient historians even credited a night of Pan-induced chaos with helping the Athenians rout the Persians at Marathon. The word passed into Latin and French before settling into English as a noun for sudden, contagious fear.

definition: A dangerously seductive person or thing that lures others toward disaster; also, a loud warning device.
origin: Siren comes from the Greek Seirenes, mythical creatures — part woman, part bird — who sang so irresistibly that sailors steered their ships onto the rocks to reach them. In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus survives their song only by having his crew plug their ears and lash him to the mast. The name later attached to any dangerous allure, and in the 19th century French inventors borrowed it again for the wailing warning device.

definition: Boldly creative or defiantly innovative, especially in a way that challenges authority or convention; relating to Prometheus.
origin: Promethean honors Prometheus, the Titan who defied Zeus by stealing fire from the gods and giving it to humanity, enabling civilization, craft, and progress. For his rebellion he was chained to a rock where an eagle devoured his regenerating liver every day for eternity. Writers from the Romantic era onward, most famously Mary Shelley in the subtitle of Frankenstein ("The Modern Prometheus"), used his name for any act of bold, transgressive creation or defiance of higher authority.

definition: Describing a task that is endless and futile, requiring continuous effort with no hope of completion.
origin: Sisyphean comes from Sisyphus, a cunning king punished in the underworld for repeatedly cheating death, condemned for eternity to push a massive boulder up a hill only to watch it roll back down each time he neared the top. The philosopher Albert Camus later used his myth as a symbol of the human condition, arguing that one must imagine Sisyphus happy despite the futility of his task. The adjective entered English use for any endlessly repeating, unwinnable labor.

definition: In Greek myth, the first mortal woman, whose curiosity led her to release all the world's evils from a sealed jar; figuratively, a source of unexpected trouble once opened.
origin: Pandora was fashioned by the gods as the first woman, given gifts by each Olympian — her name means "all-gifted" — and sent to earth carrying a sealed jar (later mistranslated as a box) she was forbidden to open. Overcome by curiosity, she lifted the lid and released disease, sorrow, and every other evil into the world, managing to trap only Hope inside before sealing it again. The phrase "opening Pandora's box" entered English for any action that unleashes irreversible trouble.

definition: A fire-breathing hybrid monster in Greek myth with a lion's head, a goat's body, and a serpent's tail; figuratively, an unrealistic hope or fanciful, unattainable idea.
origin: The Chimera was a monstrous creature in Greek myth, part lion, part goat, and part serpent, breathing fire from the goat's head that sprouted from its back, terrorizing the region of Lycia until the hero Bellerophon slew it while riding the winged horse Pegasus. Because the beast fused three incompatible animals into one impossible body, its name became the English word for any wildly implausible fantasy, and later for an organism made of genetically distinct tissues.

definition: A person or agency believed to give wise, authoritative, or divinely inspired counsel or prophecy; the place where such counsel is given.
origin: Oracle comes from Latin oraculum (a divine announcement), from orare (to speak, pray), but the concept is inseparable from the Greek Oracle of Delphi, where the priestess Pythia sat above a chasm in an entranced state and delivered cryptic prophecies believed to come directly from Apollo. Kings and generals across the ancient world traveled to consult her before major decisions, and her often riddling answers gave English the sense of an oracle as any source of profound but ambiguous wisdom.

definition: A multi-headed serpent monster in Greek myth that grew two new heads for every one severed; figuratively, a problem that multiplies when partially confronted.
origin: The Hydra of Lerna was a monstrous, many-headed serpent in Greek myth, and Heracles' second labor was to kill it, only to discover that for every head he cut off, two more grew in its place. He finally succeeded with his nephew Iolaus, who cauterized each stump with fire before it could regrow, while Heracles severed and buried the one immortal head beneath a boulder. The myth gave English the word for any problem that seems to worsen and multiply the moment it is partly solved.

definition: A wild, drunken celebration or riotous festivity; a participant in such revelry.
origin: Bacchanal comes from Bacchus, the Roman name for Dionysus, the Greek god of wine, ecstasy, and ritual madness, whose festivals featured uninhibited drinking, music, and dancing meant to dissolve ordinary restraint. Ancient Bacchanalia grew so notorious for excess that the Roman Senate moved to suppress them in 186 BC, fearing the secretive, unruly gatherings threatened public order. The word survives in English for any similarly uninhibited, drunken revelry.

definition: In Greek myth, one of the rivers of the underworld, often called the river of woe, across which the dead were ferried.
origin: The Acheron was one of the five rivers of the Greek underworld, its name traditionally linked to Greek words for "woe" or "pain," and in many accounts it was the very river the ferryman Charon rowed the dead across rather than the Styx, the two rivers often blurred together in later literature. A real river in northwestern Greece bears the same name and was long believed by ancient travelers to be an actual entrance to the underworld. The name became poetic shorthand in English for the underworld itself, or for death's threshold.
